title: Template or a designed site
metaTitle: When a website template starts to lie
excerpt: A template is a fair start when the offer is ordinary and speed matters. It fails when the product is specific and the template's sections are not true.
alt: A pale beach at sunrise, with small waves washing onto the sand and palm trees in the distance, a simple scene that does not need extra sections.
caption: A simple shore with nothing added for effect. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: When is a website template a sound choice?
faqs.answer: Use a template when the offer is a familiar shape, you can delete every section that is not true, and you need a clear page more than a distinctive one. Remove unused sections before you publish. Keep the copy, the images, and the domain in accounts you control.

faqs.question: When does a template start to misrepresent the company?
faqs.answer: It misrepresents you when its sections imply products, proof, or pricing you do not have. A specific product forced into a generic feature grid will grow extra features in the reader's mind. Delete those sections even if the page looks shorter.

faqs.question: What is a designed site, if it is not decoration?
faqs.answer: It is a set of sections chosen for this offer: a sentence a stranger can repeat, real proof, and a navigation that lists what you actually do. The visual system can be small. The work is the structure, then the build.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Website template vs custom design is a choice about whether your offer is ordinary. A template is a fair tool when the offer is a familiar one and you need the site up more than you need it to be unmistakable. It fails when the product is specific and the template's sections are lying about what you do.

The lie is usually polite. A hero with a dashboard screenshot you do not have. A logo row. A three-column feature grid full of words that could belong to any tool. The page looks finished. A stranger still cannot tell what you sell.

## When a template is an honest choice

A template is honest when the business is legible in a common shape. A restaurant with hours, a menu, and an address. A studio with a short portfolio and a way to write in. A fund with a thesis in one paragraph and a contact. The sections match the facts you already have.

Use a template when these are true:

- You can fill every visible section with something true, or you can delete the section.
- Speed matters more than distinction for this season. You are raising, opening, or simply tired of a broken page.
- The people editing will keep using that template's structure instead of fighting it with pasted code.
- Your competitors being recognizable as the same kind of company is acceptable, even useful.

Buy the template, remove half of it, and publish. A template with unused sections left "for later" is how the lie starts. Later does not come. The empty testimonial slider stays, and someone fills it with adjectives.

Put the license and the login in the company's name. Keep the font files and the logo outside the template, in a folder you can find. If the template host disappears, you should still have the mark, the copy, and the photographs. The layout is the part you are renting.

This is a good path for a weekend when the alternative is no site. A clear ordinary page beats a brilliant redesign that is still a file. Say the offer, show the proof you really have, and give one way to respond. Then stop.

## When the sections are lying

The sections lie when they imply a company you are not. Three pricing tiers and you have one offer. A blog and you have no essays. A "trusted by" row and you have two pilots who have not agreed to be named. An app screenshot from the template's demo.

Specific products suffer first. The template was drawn for a generic tool: a hero, three features, a quote, a call to action. Your product might be one narrow workflow. Forcing it into three features invents two features. Visitors will ask about those, and sales will spend the call walking them back.

Hard-to-explain products suffer next. The template offers a short headline slot and a subhead. If the truth needs a picture with labels, or a before-and-after, the slot will be filled with a slogan instead. The page will look like the template's demo with your logo swapped in. People have seen that demo. They will pattern-match you to it and then be disappointed or confused. Both cost you the conversation.

[Nielsen Norman Group's research on how long people stay](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) is blunt about the window you have. Users often leave in the first 10 to 20 seconds. The average visit lasts a little less than a minute, and people have time to read only about a quarter of the words. To earn a longer look, the value has to be clear within about 10 seconds. A template that spends those seconds on a generic claim has used up the only attention you were likely to get.

Delete before you decorate. If a section is not true, remove it. A short page that only says true things will outperform a long template that says fashionable ones. Distinction is not a custom illustration. Distinction is the absence of sections that belong to someone else.

## What ordinary means

Ordinary is not an insult. It means a stranger already has a slot in their head for you. "We design and build websites for founders" can fit a familiar studio shape. "We reconcile timber certificates for mills in one region" cannot. The first can start from a template and still be clear. The second will be bent by the template until it sounds like consulting in general.

Read the template's default headline aloud and put your facts in it. Then read the filled page to someone who does not work with you, and stop at twenty seconds. Ask them what the company does. If they repeat a feature the template invented, that feature has already become your offer in public. Remove it before you spend a month on color. If the sentence still means something, you are in the honest case. If you have to keep their structure and abandon your noun, you are in the lying case. Your noun is the product, the material, the user, the place. Keep the noun even if you keep nothing else.

Look at the navigation the template suggests. Features, solutions, resources, company, login. That set assumes a certain company. If you are a product with one login and a manual, you may need three of those links. The other two will dilute the offer. A designed site starts by refusing the links. A template can also refuse them, if you are willing to look unfinished by the template's standard. Looking unfinished by a template's standard is often looking finished to a buyer.

Wabisabi, a public Hanabi project, is a calm brand site. The useful lesson is the room it needed: quiet pages that match a specific offer, not a generic agency grid with the name changed. Thomas Bewick, an editorial site for a heritage craft brand, makes the same point in a different material. A craft archive does not fit a startup template's feature columns. The structure had to follow the work.

## A designed site is a set of decisions

Custom design, in this context, does not mean ornament. It means the sections were chosen for this offer. The first screen says who it is for and what happens next. The proof is real. The navigation is the list of things you do. The type and color are a small system you can repeat, not a theme you hope to outgrow.

The work can still be small. A designed site for an early company might be five pages. The design is the decision of which five, and what each one must accomplish. Figma is a fine place to make those decisions visible before anyone builds them. Illustrator is a fine place for the mark. Neither file is the site. The site is the built pages, in whatever tool you chose after the structure was true.

Hanabi's production build is Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind, hosted on Vercel, when the site should be code. The design can start in Framer when you want to feel the page in the browser. The order is the point. Structure first, then the tool. A template reverses that: the tool arrives with a structure, and you negotiate your company down until it fits.

Budget the design for the decisions, not for a presentation. You need a headline that a stranger can repeat, a way to show the product or the work, and a contact path. You need the mobile frame, because that is where the 10-second judgment often happens. You do not need a forty-screen brand world to replace a template. A small identity, held consistently, is enough until the offer itself changes.

## How to choose this month

Answer three questions on paper.

1. Can you delete every template section that is not true and still have a page?
2. Can a stranger repeat the offer after one short visit?
3. Will distinction change the buyer's behavior this season, or do you mostly need to exist clearly?

If the first answer is yes and the third is "we need to exist," use the template and delete aggressively. If the first answer is no, design the page. The template will keep reintroducing the lie every time you add a section from its library.

If you are midway, do a single designed homepage and keep the rest on the template only if the rest is true. A hybrid that is honest is fine. A hybrid that is a custom hero welded to a demo pricing page is the lie with better type.

## Leave yourself a way out

Plan the exit even if you start on a template. Keep copy in a document. Keep images in a folder with names. Keep the domain and the analytics in your accounts. You can move to a designed site later without a rescue operation. You cannot move easily if the only version of the words is trapped inside a visual builder's boxes.

Replacing a template is not a rebrand by default. It is a structural edit. Change the sections that lie. Keep the name, the proof, and the contact path stable so you do not throw away recognition you have already earned.

The same choice shows up when you hire. One studio can hold the design and the build so the sections do not get translated by a second team. Splitting those roles is sometimes right, and it always adds a step. That is the next question: [one studio or split design and development](/blog/one-studio-or-split-design-and-development).

Pages that had to be designed for a specific offer are collected with the rest of Hanabi's [selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works).
